storylines.label: Diffusion Language
storylines.latest_title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents

prior_narrative.tldr: Diffusion language models first appeared here as the backbone of a tool-using chemistry agent. Days later they turned up on the offensive side, as a way to craft fluent black-box attacks on LLMs.
prior_narrative.whats_new: A new paper distills a decoding schedule so diffusion LLMs commit tokens in fewer rounds, targeting the parallel-generation speedup that has been hard to realize.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Diffusion LLMs only pay off for serving if parallel decoding cuts rounds without hurting quality; this is research-stage evidence, not a deployable runtime.

status.detail: Three arXiv papers, no production release: agents, attacks and decoding speed are each explored once.

beats.headline: Masked diffusion LMs drive a tool-integrated chemistry agent
Diffusion LMs used for perplexity-aware black-box attacks
Schedule distillation aims to cut dLLM decoding rounds

open_questions: Do the schedule-distillation speedups hold on independent benchmarks at equal output quality?
Does any inference framework or vendor ship diffusion LLM serving with parallel decoding?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Do not plan serving capacity around diffusion LLMs yet; if you prototype one, measure decoding rounds and quality against your autoregressive baseline, and include fluent-prompt attacks in red-team evals.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: EnvSched: Environment-Aware Scheduling for Rollout-Efficient Agent Reinforcement Learning

prior_narrative.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of RL items, not one developing story. Since Oct 12 it has gathered a Qwen long-horizon agent report, an O-RAN benchmark, agentic-RL training papers, and AWS's SageMaker guide.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Oct 26: three arXiv papers turn RL on agent failures: MiRL targets terminal-agent misbehaviors, CalibraRL targets RAG hallucinations, and a video-editing study shows fine-grained credit can hurt.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: The newest papers frame RL as a reliability tool: train against named failures (MiRL), reward calibrated abstention (CalibraRL), and test whether per-step credit helps (it can hurt). All are paper-reported results, not production evidence; the SageMaker guide remains the only managed-platform recipe.

status.detail: A loose set of RL items; the newest aim RL at agent reliability and credit-assignment limits.

beats.summary: Reported via MarkTechPost; targets agent tasks that run far longer than standard RL rollouts.

beats.summary: Targets O-RAN controllers rather than LLM post-training.

beats.headline: Agentic RL papers: rollout budgets, stateful environments, search-state awareness, credit assignment
beats.summary: Four arXiv papers on cutting rollout cost, extending RL beyond tool-centric settings, teaching search agents to assess their own state, and crediting individual decisions within an episode.

beats.headline: AWS multi-turn RL guide, plus stability, simulation, robustness and token-credit papers
beats.summary: A managed-platform recipe on SageMaker AI and four arXiv papers on rounding alignment, token credit, dialogue user simulation and robust RL.

beats.headline: Reliability turn: calibrated rewards, credit-assignment limits, error-targeted agent fixes
beats.summary: Oct 26: three arXiv papers aim RL at hallucination, when fine-grained credit hurts, and terminal-agent misbehavior.

open_questions: Does calibrated rollout budgeting cut MCP-agent training cost on benchmarks beyond the paper's own?
Does Qwen publish QwenGyre weights, code, or benchmarks that show the elastic RL gain on long-horizon agent tasks?
Does the SageMaker MTRL recipe carry from Wordle to tool-using agent tasks, and at what training cost?
Does twin-world credit assignment improve agent training on benchmarks beyond the paper's own?
Does rounding-location alignment stabilize RL training outside the paper's own setups?
Do MiRL's error-targeted fixes hold on terminal-agent tasks outside the paper's own benchmark?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you train tool-using agents, log recurring failure modes and test error-targeted RL (MiRL) against them, and A/B fine-grained credit assignment against episode-level reward before adopting it; treat paper results as unreplicated until you rerun them on your own evals.

storylines.label: Long-term Memory
storylines.latest_title: ETAMem: Decoupling and Aligning Heterogeneous Memory for Long-Term Conversational Agents

prior_narrative.tldr: A Sep 22 post asked how to evaluate agent memory beyond the context window. PACMI (Oct 5) then shifted the focus to keeping memory correct by invalidating stale entries.
prior_narrative.whats_new: An open-source repo (Oct 11) stores coding-agent long-term memory as a tree of plain files, a simple alternative to a dedicated memory service.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Agents that persist memory across sessions need an update and invalidation policy, not only a retrieval layer; plain-file stores make that state inspectable and diffable, but give you no invalidation for free.

status.detail: Memory work spans evaluation, invalidation research, and lightweight file-based implementations for coding agents.

beats.headline: A benchmark post asks how to evaluate memory beyond context windows
PACMI cascades invalidation through provenance-linked memories
beats.summary: Targets memories that become outdated as new observations arrive.

beats.headline: Coding-agent memory as a tree of plain files
beats.summary: An open-source repo implements long-term memory without a dedicated store.

open_questions: Does PACMI's invalidation cascade hold up on an independent long-horizon agent benchmark?
Will any file-based memory store publish results on stale-memory handling?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If your agent persists memory across sessions, record where each memory came from and test that correcting one fact also retires memories derived from it, whatever the storage backend.

prior_narrative.tldr: This page groups items by the shared phrase "large language models"; they do not form one developing story. Oct 9-22 items cover knowledge graphs, sycophancy, code-translation hallucinations, search agents, and spectral edits.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Oct 26 adds a long-horizon web-search benchmark with failure-node localization, a neuron-steering method, self-evolving KG reasoning, and Reva, a real-time vulnerability detector for generated code.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Treat this as a reading list, not a thread. For platform engineers the useful items are LongSearchEval (agent failure localization) and Reva (screening agent-written code), plus the code-translation hallucination catalog.

open_questions: Does independent replication confirm the spectral-intervention capability shifts?
Do the code-translation mitigations hold on languages outside the paper's test set?
Does Reva's real-time screening keep false positives low enough to gate agent-written code?
Does CANS steering preserve general capability on models beyond those it was tested on?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you run coding agents, read Reva and check whether per-function vulnerability screening could sit before review; if you run search agents, try LongSearchEval's failure-node localization on your traces. Skip the rest unless it matches your domain.
